references.text: The sick man's answer presupposes the context of John 5:3-4, where many sick people lay by the pool waiting for the water to be stirred up, because the first one who stepped down after that was healed.
In John 5:5-6, the man's condition is described—he had been sick for 38 years—and Jesus asks if he wants to get well, which leads to this answer where he explains his helplessness.
Jesus' healing of the man in John 5:8-9 stands in contrast to the man's experience of being without help; Jesus intervenes where no one else could help.
In John 9:1-7, Jesus heals a man born blind at the Pool of Siloam, a similar situation where a helpless person encounters Jesus' healing power at a water place in Jerusalem.
In Mark 2:3-5, a paralyzed man is carried to Jesus by friends, in contrast to the man at Bethesda who complains that he has no one to help him into the pool.
Isaiah 25:4 describes the Lord as a refuge for the helpless and weak, which mirrors the sick man's situation where he is without human help until the Lord Himself intervenes.
In Psalm 142:5, the psalmist cries out that no one cares about him and that he has no place of refuge—a complaint about helplessness similar to the sick man's words that he has no one to help him.
Psalm 22:12 expresses a prayer to God not to be far away because there is no helper—a parallel to the man's complaint about lacking human assistance.
In Acts 3:1-8, a paralyzed man who was carried daily to the temple gate is healed, a similar situation involving long-term sickness and helplessness overcome by divine intervention.
